passages.original: Varronem: namque hunc fama est impellere signa.
passages.english: Varro: for rumour has it that he is the one driving the standards forward.
passages.notes: The accusative 'Varronem' depends on a verb in the preceding (missing) context. 'impellere signa' may mean urging the army on to battle.

passages.original: isque ut Varronem procul inter proelia uidit
passages.english: and when he saw Varro far off amid the fighting
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete; the main clause follows in the next line. 'is' refers to someone named in the preceding context.

passages.original: Talia dum memorant, umbra ueniente Sibyllae
passages.english: While they recount such things, as the shade of the Sibyl comes on,
passages.notes: The line as given seems odd: 'umbra ueniente Sibyllae' is hard to construe and looks garbled, perhaps conflated with the following line. The translation follows the words as transmitted.

passages.original: ora Sibylla docet uenientum et nomina pandit.
passages.english: the Sibyl points out the faces of those approaching and discloses their names.

passages.original: Liuius: ‘Huc, iuuenes, huc me spectate ruentem
passages.english: Livius: 'Here, young men, here, look at me as I rush on
passages.notes: 'Liuius' seems to be a speaker label or name heading, possibly not part of the verse; it presumably refers to a Livius among the shades. The quotation continues beyond this line.
